text: FMD in cattle is caused by a virus (antibiotics don't work); strains O, A, and Asia1 have been identified in Cambodia. The virus can spread from pigs to cattle, since pigs shed very high amounts of virus and cattle are very susceptible to airborne infection. Symptoms: fever and loss of appetite (from both the fever and painful mouth vesicles); vesicles on the tongue, dental pad, gums, and lips (lip lesions are rare in pigs) causing heavy salivation; blister lesions at the coronary band and between the toes make infected animals sway from foot to foot from tenderness; vesicles can also appear on the teats and udder; calf deaths are common from heart muscle (myocardium) damage. Treatment: none directly (viral), and vaccinating an already-sick animal doesn't help; treatment aims to prevent secondary bacterial infection — inject TMP+Sulfa or OTC for 5–7 days, wash foot lesions with soap, then spray a disinfectant combining Gentian Violet and OTC after cleaning; since the animal can't walk, eat, or drink normally, provide grass and rice bran mash plus water within reach, and keep it shaded to reduce dehydration. Prevention: vaccinate twice a year with the trivalent (O+A+Asia1) vaccine; cattle develop immunity quickly after vaccination, so it's worth vaccinating immediately on hearing of suspected cases nearby, though vaccine doses can be hard to source quickly once an outbreak is already spreading and suppliers run low.
